# Myeloid cells mediate interferon-driven resistance to immunotherapy in advanced renal cell carcinoma

**Authors:** Kevin Bi; Soki Kashima; Sabrina Y. Camp; Kevin Meli; Eddy Saad; Breanna M. Titchen; Chris Labaki; Ziad Bakouny; Erica M. Pimenta; Jihye Park; Erin Shannon; Jingxin Fu; Sherin Xirenayi; Jack Horst; Lotus Lum; Jeffrey J. Ishizuka; Toni K. Choueiri; David A. Braun; Eliezer M. Van Allen

## Abstract

Sustained type-I and type-II interferon (IFN) signaling can drive multiple mechanisms of resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Here, we used single cell RNA-sequencing data to characterize the effects of IFNs in the tumor-immune microenvironment (TME) of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), then examined how IFN-driven cellular phenotypes modulate ICB efficacy. Using mixed-effects models, we inferred the IFN-inducibility of putative interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) within cell types. Genes encoding inhibitory ligands and immune checkpoints were strongly expressed and IFN-inducible in macrophages, but less so in RCC tumor cells. In orthogonal clinical trial cohorts, a signature of myeloid IFNγ signaling, but not tumor IFNγ signaling, predicted primary resistance to first-line ICB plus anti-VEGF therapy. Functionally, IFNγ-conditioned macrophages inhibited T cell killing of RCC tumor cells in vitro. Our inferential modeling approach offers a framework for biomarker discovery through deconvolution of cytokine signaling effects in the TME, and points to myeloid cells as mediators of tumor-extrinsic, IFN-driven resistance to immunotherapy in RCC.

## Abstract

Bi et al. describe cell type-specific transcriptional signatures of interferon (IFN) signaling in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) tumors and examine effects on immunotherapy outcomes. They find that myeloid IFNγ signaling, but not tumor IFNγ signaling, predicts poor outcomes in clinical trial cohorts, pointing to myeloid cells as mediators of IFN-driven immunotherapy resistance in RCC.

## INTRODUCTION:

Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has become a crucial component of first-line management of advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC)1-6. However, RCC immunobiology is distinct from that of other immunotherapy-responsive cancer types. Though RCC lesions are inflamed and show high levels of cytolytic activity, intratumoral CD8 T cell density is associated with poorer prognosis7-9. Moreover, conventional ICB response biomarkers established in melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) fail to reliably stratify outcomes in RCC. Tumor mutational burden (TMB), measures of T cell abundance and function, and PD-L1 expression have proven inconsistent as predictive biomarkers in RCC patients10. These findings call for a deeper understanding of how baseline inflammation in the microenvironment may modulate the capacity for response to current ICB regimens.

Under chronic conditions, type-I and type-II interferon (IFN) signaling can drive negative feedback mechanisms to suppress antitumor immunity. These include dampening of TNF-mediated tumor cell death and upregulation of IDO1, IL10, PD-L1, and other inhibitory ligands in tumor and immune subsets11,12. In several cancer types, disruption of IFN signaling potently sensitizes tumors to checkpoint blockade. Tumor-specific ablation of IFN signaling in mouse models of melanoma, colorectal cancer, and breast cancer improves ICB response and overcomes acquired resistance11,13-15. In NSCLC, for a subset of patients with no initial response to anti-PD-1 monotherapy, intermittent addition of the JAK inhibitor itacitinib can enhance CD8 T cell plasticity through ablation of IFN signaling and potentiate an objective response16.

In RCC, the relationship between IFNs and ICB outcomes is unclear, with conflicting evidence between murine models and patient clinical data. ICB response in the Renca syngeneic model depends on a fast on/fast off program of type-I IFN (IFNα/β) activation, whereas non-responding tumors show chronic activation of the pathway over time17. Type-II IFN (IFNγ) induces ICB resistance in Renca through tumoral expression of the inhibitory ligand Qa-1/HLA-E18. However, in RCC patient data, a broad IFNγ signaling signature is not significantly predictive of resistance to anti-PD-1 in a multivariate analysis, and tumor mutations in core IFNγ pathway genes are not associated with altered response18,19. Indeed, efforts in this cancer type and others have largely focused on the role of tumor-specific IFN signaling in promoting resistance, while the contribution of immune and stromal-expressed interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) to T cell suppression is poorly understood. Notably, RCC lesions are rich in macrophages expressing a host of inhibitory ligands, some of which are upregulated by malignant cells of other cancer types during IFN-induced acquired resistance13,20,21. We therefore propose that a more complete understanding of ISG expression in this disease is necessary to accurately model outcomes under checkpoint blockade.

In this study, we explored correlates of IFN signaling in RCC at single cell resolution. By inferring the IFN-inducibility of genes within each cell type, we defined strict signatures describing cell type-specific type-I and type-II responses. We then looked to larger clinical trial cohorts to model effects on first-line ICB-containing treatment regimens that align with current standard of care. Our results point to a tumor-extrinsic mechanism of IFNγ-driven primary resistance mediated by myeloid cells, and highlight the importance of considering cell type-specificity during biomarker discovery.

## RESULTS:

### A multi-cohort scRNA-seq dataset reveals patterns of ISG expression in RCC

The tumor-immune microenvironment of RCC is highly variable with disease stage and ICB exposure status. We therefore integrated single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from three independent studies20-22 to achieve representation across these clinical characteristics, arriving at a combined dataset of 42 RCC tumor samples from 27 patients (Methods). These samples spanned lesions from early stage (n = 5), locally advanced (n = 12), and metastatic (n = 25) disease, and from ICB-naive (n = 24) and ICB-exposed tumors (n = 18) (Figure 1A, 1B). Following quality control and cell type annotation, 228,371 cells from 14 broad cell types (tumor, fibroblast, perivascular, endothelial, tumor-associated macrophage (TAM), monocyte, DC, CD8, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, T-reg, B cell, and plasma cell), each with representation from all three originating cohorts, were retained for subsequent analysis (Figure 1C, S1A, S1B, Table S1A-C).

Previous work in other disease types identified two non-overlapping sets of ISGs, termed ISG.RS (expressed primarily by tumor cells) and IFNG.GS (expressed preferentially by immune cells)14,15. In melanoma, ISG.RS predicts resistance to ICB, while IFNG.GS predicts response14. To investigate whether these broad patterns of ISG expression were conserved in RCC, we scored cells in our dataset for ISG.RS and IFNG.GS gene signatures. We found that in RCC samples, IFNG.GS was enriched in myeloid cells relative to tumor, stromal, and lymphoid lineages, corroborating patterns observed in melanoma14 (Figure 1D, S2A). Also consistent with other studies, ISG.RS was enriched in tumor cells compared to lymphoid cells14. However, stromal cells exhibited far greater levels of ISG.RS expression than tumor cells, and of the 38 individual genes comprising ISG.RS, few showed tumor-specific patterns of expression (Figure 1D, S2B). This may in part explain prior observations that in RCC bulk RNA-seq data, ISG.RS does not strongly predict low CD8+ T cell cytolytic activity15, as high stromal expression convolutes the specificity of the signature as a measure of IFN signaling in cancer cells. Furthermore, IFNG.GS/ISG.RS did not consistently predict ICB outcomes in RCC (Figure S2C-F). We therefore aimed to refine these signatures by focusing on cell type specificity, surmising that this could yield more clinically informative measures of IFN signaling.

To identify patterns of ISG expression in the RCC microenvironment, we performed differential expression analysis between each cell type and all other cell types for a set of 259 putative ISGs, defined as the union of genes from ISG.RS, IFNG.GS, hallmark IFNα and IFNγ gene sets, and a curated set of immune checkpoints and immune evasion genes (Methods, Table S1D). We found that many ISGs were enriched in specific cell types, but also in certain groupings of cell types. For example, the genes C1S, SERPING1, and C1R were highly enriched in tumor cells but also expressed in fibroblasts and perivascular cells (Figure 1E). Other putative ISGs, such as HLA-DRA, CXCL10, VSIG4, VSIR, and IRF8 were most strongly expressed by either TAMs, monocytes, or DCs, but also showed generally higher expression in all myeloid cells relative to other cell types. Another subset of genes, including CCL5, GZMA, OASL, ITGB7, and CD69, was enriched across T and NK cells, with varying expression between CD8s, NKs, and T-helper cells. Thus, in RCC, ISG expression is not well dichotomized into tumor versus immune, exhibiting more complex patterns of specificity across cell lineages and types.

### Inferring the type-I and type-II IFN-inducibility of putative ISGs

Many of these putative ISGs are regulated by a host of stimuli beyond IFNs, or are differentially expressed at baseline between some cell types regardless of IFN signaling23-25. We therefore devised an approach to infer the IFN-inducibility of putative ISGs in our dataset, aiming to more rigorously define a subset of these genes as IFN-driven in this disease context. First, we used CytoSig, a database and toolset for measuring cytokine signaling in transcriptional data, to quantify type-I and type-II IFN response at single cell resolution26. Importantly, we applied CytoSig to each cell type individually, assuming that although the reference database incorporates ISGs from many different experimental settings, scores calculated within a given cell type accurately reflect relative levels of IFN signaling. Next, for each gene, we fit a linear mixed effects model within cells of a given cell type to predict expression as a function of IFNα/β CytoSig score, IFNγ CytoSig score, number of genes expressed per cell, early (I/II) versus late (III/IV) disease stage, and patient of origin (Methods). Under this model, β coefficients for IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores serve as measures of the effect of IFN signaling on a gene’s expression.

Examining the top genes skewed towards type-I or type-II inducibility in tumor cells, TAMs, and CD8s, we found that genes canonically induced by IFNα/β, such as MX1, MX2, ISG15, IFI6, IFIT1, IFIT3, OAS1, EIF2AK2, and DDX58 emerged consistently as type-I-skewed15,27-31 (Figure 1F, Table S2A-S2M). Likewise, genes known to be preferentially induced by IFNγ, including IRF1, GBP2, PSMB10, PSMB8, IDO1, and VAMP5, were type-II-skewed32-37 (Figure 1F, Table S2A-S2M). Thus, our CytoSig-based approach to quantifying IFN signaling and inferring ISG inducibility was sensitive to differences between type-I and type-II pathway activation.

### CD8 LAG3-Hi cells are the primary source of IFNγ in RCC tumors

Although CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells broadly express IFNG transcript in RCC (Figure S3A), transcript levels for cytokines at single cell resolution are generally poorly descriptive of protein expression38,39. By leveraging CytoSig scores for IFNγ signaling across samples, we sought to systematically identify the cell types or subtypes most responsible for potentiating type-II IFN signaling across the microenvironment.

Briefly, for each cell type, we calculated the median IFNγ CytoSig score within each sample. We then fit a multiple linear regression model to predict this score using sample-level proportions of CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells, percentage of IFNG+ cells in each cell type, as well as median IFNα/β CytoSig score to adjust for type-I-driven effects (Methods). CD8 proportion, and to a lesser extent NK cell proportion, significantly predicted type-II IFN signaling in multiple cell types (Figure S3B, S3C). We applied a similar approach to predict median IFNα/β CytoSig scores using myeloid, tumor, and stromal cell proportions as model covariates, but found that no broad cell type frequency was consistently predictive of type-I IFN signaling (Methods, Figure S3D-S3F).

We next aimed to narrow down the source of IFNγ to granular CD8 subsets. We focused on five subsets with adequate cell numbers: CD8 41BB-Hi (terminally exhausted, marked by TOX40,41, TNFRSF920, CXCL1342, and ENTPD143), CD8 LAG3-Hi (intermediate exhausted, marked by PDCD1, LAG3, HAVCR244,45, and GZMB46,47), CD8 HSP-Hi (marked by heat shock protein genes and highest IFNG expression), CD8 ISG-Hi (marked by high expression of type-I ISGs such as MX127 and ISG1528), and CD8 IL7R-Hi (resident memory or effector memory, marked by IL7R48, ITGAE49, ZNF68350, and KLRG147) (Figure S4A-S4C, Table S1B). We again fit multiple linear regression models for predicting IFNγ CytoSig score within each cell type using CD8 subset proportions, percentage of IFNG+ cells in each subset, and IFNα/β CytoSig score as covariates.

We found that only the proportion of CD8 LAG3-Hi (intermediate exhausted) cells was a significant predictor of type-II IFN signaling in most cell types (Figure 2A). Percent IFNG positivity generally failed to predict type-II response levels, as did the proportion of CD8 HSP-Hi cells, the subset with the highest average IFNG expression. Notably, this CD8 HSP-Hi subset expressed lower levels of inhibitory receptor genes relative to CD8 LAG3-Hi cells, possibly suggesting lower tumor-reactivity (Figure S4C). CD8 41BB-Hi cells, exhibiting hallmarks of terminal exhaustion, also had no predicted effect on type-II IFN signaling, reflecting hypofunction associated with prolonged antigen exposure. Thus, CD8 LAG3-Hi cells, which show co-expression of multiple inhibitory receptors but only moderate levels of TOX and ENTPD1 – characteristic of intermediate exhaustion – are likely to be the primary source of IFNγ in RCC tumors.

### TAMs are responsive to IFNγ from CD8 LAG3-Hi cells and express IFN-inducible immune checkpoints

Among all broad cell types, TAMs expressed the highest levels of IFNGR1 and IFNGR2, and type-II IFN signaling in TAMs was strongly predicted by CD8 LAG3-Hi proportion across samples (Figure 2A, 2B). Moreover, TAMs in RCC express several immune checkpoints upregulated by tumor cells of other cancers during IFN-driven acquired resistance13,20,21. We therefore examined TAM phenotypes in settings of high and low CD8 LAG3-Hi frequency.

We found that in lesions from late-stage disease with a high proportion of CD8 LAG3-Hi cells, TAMs were polarized towards a CXCL10-Hi phenotype (Figure 2C, 2D, S4D-G). Relative to other TAM subtypes, TAM CXCL10-Hi cells showed increased IFNγ and IFNα/β CytoSig scores and elevated expression of immune checkpoint genes, including CD274 and PDCD1LG2 (encoding PD-L1 and PD-L2), LGALS9 (encoding Gal-9, a TIM3 ligand), NECTIN2 (encoding CD112, a TIGIT ligand), TNFRSF14 (encoding HVEM, a BTLA ligand), CD80 (encoding a CTLA4 ligand), and LILRB1 (encoding a receptor for HLA molecules and negative regulator of phagocytosis)51-53 (Figure 2E, Table S1C).

Indeed, many of these genes are elevated in the tumor microenvironment during checkpoint blockade and have been linked to acquired resistance13. However, given that RCC lesions show high baseline levels of inflammation, we surmised that IFN signaling might drive substantial variability in immune checkpoint gene expression even in a pre-treatment setting. We therefore applied our approach for inferring IFN-inducibility of putative ISGs to cells from ICB-naive tumors only (Table S3A-S3M).

We observed that in TAMs from untreated lesions, LGALS9, LGALS3 (encoding Gal-3, a LAG3 ligand)54, and VSIG4 (encoding a macrophage-specific B7 family protein)55 were significantly associated with type-I IFN signaling (Figure 2F, Table S3A-S3M). VSIR (encoding VISTA)56,57, SIGLEC10 (encoding a receptor for CD24 and anti-phagocytotic checkpoint)58,59, TNFRSF14, CD80, CD86, CD274, PDCD1LG2, and NECTIN2 were associated with type-II IFN signaling (Figure 2F, Table S3A-S3M). With the exception of CD274, PDCD1LG2, and CD80, these genes were expressed abundantly in TAMs across patients, with a median percent expression of at least 40%.

In contrast, RCC tumor cells from ICB-naive lesions showed low levels of expression for most of these immune checkpoint genes. Among significantly IFN-inducible genes, only TNFRSF14, CD47, and NECTIN2 were expressed at a median percentage of at least 20% across patients (Figure 2F). CD274, PDCD1LG2, CEACAM1, and LGALS9, although significantly associated with type-I and/or type-II IFN signaling, each showed less than 5% median expression in tumor cells across patients. Overall, these findings indicate that TAMs, and to a lesser extent tumor cells, express IFN-driven genes which could represent mechanisms of immune evasion active in the microenvironment prior to ICB therapy.

### Derivation of signatures for quantifying cell type-specific IFN signaling in clinically integrated bulk RNA sequencing data

We next aimed to examine the effects of IFN signaling on clinical outcomes under ICB-containing treatment regimens in larger orthogonal cohorts of RCC patients. To this end, we first leveraged our single cell dataset to define strict gene sets describing cell type-specific type-I and type-II IFN signaling at pre-treatment baseline (Figure 3A).

Using cells from ICB-naive patients only, we performed a series of pairwise one-versus-each differential expression tests between a given cell type and all other unrelated cell types. From this analysis, a gene was considered cell type-specific (CTS) if it passed cutoffs for significant enrichment in all pairwise tests (Methods). Because some groups of cell types, for instance myeloid cells, exhibited similar ISG expression patterns (Figure S5A, S5B), we disregarded within-group pairwise tests (e.g. TAM versus monocyte) in calling CTS genes.

Next, we identified the overlap of CTS genes with significantly type-I or type-II-inducible genes in each cell type from ICB-naive patients. As an additional step to screen against genes without prior biological evidence for involvement in IFN signaling, this overlapping set was filtered to exclude genes not appearing in our putative ISG set. Using this approach, we identified key IFN-driven genes expressed preferentially by cell types in RCC. In TAMs, type-II ISGs included CXCL9, TNFAIP2, JAK2, CD86, SIGLEC10, and IL15, and type-I ISGs included MX2, VSIG4, IFI30, and IL10 (Figure 3B). In tumor cells, C1S, CFB, and SSPN were type-II-driven, while TNFAIP6 and PFKP were type-I-driven. In T-helper cells, STAT4, XCL1, and IL2RB were type-I-driven, while CCL5 and GZMA were notably driven by both type-I and type-II IFN.

Given concordant patterns of ISG expression across certain groups of cell types, CTS ISGs were then combined within these groups to arrive at finalized gene signatures (Figure S5C, Table S1D). For the purpose of this analysis, TAMs, monocytes, and DCs formed one group (myeloid), and CD8, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, and T-reg formed another (T/NK) (Figure S5A). We also found that tumor-expressed ISGs tended to be robustly detected in fibroblasts (Figure S5B) – therefore, tumor cells and fibroblasts/perivascular cells were also considered as a group (tumor/fibroblast). Signature scores for these CTS ISG gene sets in cells from untreated patients were, as expected, enriched in the cell types of interest and elevated in cells with high levels of type-I or type-II IFN signaling (Figure S5D).

To assess the generalizability of these gene sets in measuring cell type-specific IFN signaling, we scored samples in our dataset from previously treated patients, not included during signature derivation, for all CTS ISG signatures. We found that even among samples from treated patients, our myeloid IFNγ and IFNα/β signatures were enriched in TAMs, monocytes, and DCs with high IFNγ and IFNα/β CytoSig scores respectively, and showed low levels of detection in other cell types (Figure 3C, 3D). Likewise, our tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signature was enriched in tumor cells and fibroblasts with high IFN response, but was detected at low levels in other cell types (Figure 3C, 3D). However, the tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β signature failed to validate in this treated set, perhaps indicating substantial inter-tumoral heterogeneity in the response to type-I IFN signaling, which would require a larger training dataset to fully appreciate.

To test the validity of our signatures in bulk data, we next calculated CTS ISG signature scores in pre-treatment bulk RNA-seq data from IMmotion151 (IM151)60-62 and JAVELIN Renal 101 (JR101)63,64, two cohorts of RCC patients treated with first-line ICB plus anti-VEGF combination regimens or single-agent sunitinib (Table S4A, S4B). We assigned samples from each cohort into four discrete bins based on IFNG expression and inferred TAM fraction (Methods) and examined the distributions of signature scores. We found that in both IM151 and JR101, the myeloid IFNγ signaling signature was strongly enriched in samples with high levels of both IFNG and TAM infiltration relative to samples that were low for either or both variables (Figure 3E). Similarly, in both cohorts, the tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling signature was most elevated in samples with high IFNG detection and high tumor cell plus fibroblast fraction (Figure 3F). These results indicate that our signatures are a reasonable proxy for cell type-specific IFN responses, and are a suitable alternative to IFNG.GS and ISG.RS as descriptors of IFN signaling in the RCC microenvironment.

### Myeloid IFNγ signaling is associated with primary resistance to ICB-containing regimens

We next sought to understand how cell type-specific IFN signaling might contribute to response or resistance to first-line standard-of-care advanced RCC therapy. Using the scores for our CTS ISG signatures (Figure S5C, Table S1D, S4A, S4B) in bulk RNA-seq data from IM151 and JR101, we fit Cox proportional hazards models for progression-free survival (PFS) in each treatment arm of the two studies, incorporating relevant immune and clinicopathological variables. Model covariates included myeloid IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, as well as TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx65 to adjust for the effect of overall cell type frequencies. We chose to exclude T/NK IFN signaling signatures in favor of a more explicit measure of CD8 T cell function in the tumor – the previously published CD8A+ tissue-resident signature described by Krishna et al. as predicting ICB response in both IM151 and JR10122. We noted, however, that this signature was derived from differential expression analysis between a single CD8 T cell subtype and all other cells, including non-T cells, limiting its phenotypic specificity; furthermore, the signature is absent of canonical tissue resident memory markers such as ITGAE (CD103) and ZNF683 (Hobit)49,50. Thus, in our analysis, we re-termed this signature as “Krishna CD8 predictive”, and regarded it as a more general signature describing CD8 T cell effector function based on genes such as CCL3, CCL4, GZMK, and IFNG66. Lastly, we also incorporated as model covariates age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity.

Strikingly, we found that pre-treatment myeloid IFNγ signaling, but not tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling, was associated with shorter PFS in patients treated with atezolizumab and bevacizumab (ICB plus anti-VEGF) in IM151 (HR = 1.59, 95% C.I. = 1.21–2.09, p < 0.001) and patients treated with avelumab and axitinib (ICB plus anti-VEGF) in JR101 (HR = 1.50, 95% C.I. = 1.04-2.18, p = 0.032) (Figure 4A, 4B). This effect was specific to the ICB-containing treatment regimens in each cohort, as myeloid IFNγ signaling did not predict longer or shorter PFS in the sunitinib (non-ICB) arm of either study (Figure S6A, S6B). We also examined this potential resistance effect using logistic regression models for predicting another clinical endpoint of efficacy, clinical benefit (CB) versus no clinical benefit (NCB) using the same set of variables (Methods). We found that myeloid IFNγ signaling was significantly associated with NCB in the ICB-containing arms of both IM151 and JR101 but not the sunitinib-treated arms (Figure S6C-S6F).

In contrast, the Krishna CD8 predictive signature was associated with clinical benefit and improved PFS under ICB in both cohorts (Figure 4A, 4B, S6C, S6D). To explicitly examine the effect of myeloid IFNγ signaling on outcomes in settings of adequate baseline CD8 T cell function, we next restricted our survival analysis to samples with meaningfully high levels of the Krishna CD8 predictive signature (Methods). Stratification of these samples by myeloid IFNγ signaling along optimal cutoffs showed that higher myeloid IFNγ signaling again predicted shorter PFS in the ICB arms of IM151 (MVA HR = 2.01, 95% C.I. = 1.24-3.24, p = 0.005) and JR101 (MVA HR = 2.84, 95% C.I. = 1.38-5.85, p = 0.005), but not the sunitinib arms (Figure 4C, 4D, S6G-S9J). Transferring optimal cutoffs for myeloid IFNγ signaling score between JR101 and IM151 yielded similar model results (Figure S6K-S6N). Thus, IFNγ signaling in myeloid cells is a significant contributor to immunotherapy resistance and may constrain CD8 T cell function in RCC.

Several myeloid-related gene signatures have been previously derived from RCC data, or have been shown to stratify therapeutic outcomes. A curated signature of myeloid inflammation has been associated with poor outcomes under single-agent atezolizumab, and to a lesser extent under atezolizumab plus bevacizumab60, but not avelumab plus axitinib64. Notably, this signature and our myeloid IFNγ signaling signature describe distinctly different biology (Figure S7A-S7D). Krishna et al. also described unsupervised clusters of TAMs defined by intermediate or high expression of HLA genes or ISGs, finding that ISG-high TAM were associated with improved PFS under sunitinib only22. Another study, from Kinget et al., identified a gene signature associated with low tumoral HLA promiscuity (tLHP) in RCC and demonstrated through stratification that higher levels of the tLHP signature predicted ICB response in JAVELIN Renal 101 and IMmotion15067. Interestingly, this tLHP signature was most enriched in myeloid cells in their scRNA-seq data, and may be related to presentation of antigen by TAMs to CD8s. We therefore aimed to compare the performance of these gene sets against that of our myeloid IFNγ signaling signature in Cox and logistic regressions to determine whether our pathway-focused approach showed convergent signal with existing signatures.

We found that when adjusting for all pertinent immune and clinical variables, only the myeloid IFNγ signaling signature was significantly associated with both shorter PFS and lack of clinical benefit under ICB in both IMmotion151 and JAVELIN Renal 101 (Methods, Figure 4E, S7E). Apart from gene sets external to this study, we also generated signatures of non-IFN-inducible TAM, monocyte, and DC-specific genes from our scRNA-seq data to test in these same models (Methods). None of these signatures were consistently associated with resistance. Thus, our measure of myeloid IFNγ signaling is a more robust indicator of ICB resistance than other RCC myeloid-related gene sets which do not directly take into account the response to interferons.

These findings contrast with recent work in other disease types, which identifies IFNγ-polarized, CXCL9+ TAMs as broadly anti-tumor (compared to pro-tumor hypoxia-polarized SPP1+ TAMs) and associated with better prognosis68. CXCL9 is present in our myeloid IFNγ signaling signature, and both CXCL9+ and SPP1+ TAMs occur in RCC (Figure S5C, S4E). However, the ratio of CXCL9 to SPP1 expression (CS ratio) does not significantly predict improved PFS under ICB in either IMmotion151 (HR = 1.20, 95% C.I. = 0.97-1.49, p = 0.101) or JAVELIN Renal 101 (HR = 0.99, 95% C.I. = 0.79-1.23, p = 0.905) (Figure S8A-S8D). IFNγ-polarization of TAMs is therefore not a marker of ICB response or better outcomes in RCC; instead, IFNγ signaling in myeloid cells is associated with ICB resistance.

### Non-myeloid IFN signaling signatures do not predict ICB outcomes

We additionally explored proposed non-myeloid mechanisms of ICB resistance in these two clinical cohorts. One prior study posited that IFNγ signaling in RCC tumor cells could drive ICB resistance through expression of the checkpoint ligand Qa-1/HLA-E, and that IFN-driven resistance was therefore dependent on an intact 6p21.3 locus18. However, this was not supported by our analysis in the JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort, where copy number data was available for tumor specimens. Neither hallmark nor tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling signatures predicted resistance to avelumab plus axitinib when adjusting for necessary clinical variables, regardless of 6p21 disomy (tumor/fib. IFNγ signaling signature; HR = 1.11, 95% C.I. = 0.92-1.35, p = 0.262) or deletion (tumor/fib. IFNγ signaling signature; HR = 1.10, 95% C.I. = 0.73-1.67, p = 0.646) (Figure S8E-S8H).

In the Renca mouse model, a fast on/fast off program of IFNβ signaling drives ICB response, while nonresponders show slow and chronic activation of a separate set of ISGs over time17. However, we found that a signature of human orthologs of the fast on/fast off program was not significantly predictive of response or resistance to ICB-containing regimens in IMmotion151 (HR = 1.01, 95% C.I. = 0.88-1.17, p = 0.854) or JAVELIN Renal 101 (HR = 1.00, 95% C.I. = 0.86-1.16, p = 0.988) (Figure S8I-S8L). Furthermore, our myeloid and tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β signaling signatures were not consistently associated with response or resistance across cohorts (Figure S8M-S8P).

Lastly, we examined the effect of a more general IFN response-related signature – the T cell-inflamed gene expression profile (GEP), which predicts response to PD-1 blockade in melanoma, head and neck cancer, and pan cancer cohorts69. This signature was also not significantly associated with response or resistance under ICB-containing regimens in IMmotion151 (HR = 0.98, 95% C.I. = 0.84-1.13, p = 0.739) or JAVELIN Renal 101 (HR = 0.96, 95% C.I. = 0.82-1.12, p = 0.609) (Figure S8Q-S8T). Thus, potential IFN-associated predictors of primary ICB outcomes derived from other cancer types or preclinical work in murine kidney cancer models are not as strongly supported by RCC clinical data as our framework based on cell type-specific IFNγ signaling.

### IFNγ-stimulated macrophages inhibit RCC tumor cell killing by antigen-specific T cells in vitro

Given that our clinically-based findings implicate myeloid cells as a mediator of IFN-driven resistance to ICB, we hypothesized that IFNγ signaling in myeloid cells could lead directly to dampened T cell function. To this end, we assessed the impact of IFNγ-stimulated macrophages on antigen-specific T cell killing of RCC tumor cells in vitro. Briefly, we induced monocyte-derived macrophages and generated T cells expressing the HLA-A*02:01-restricted NY-ESO-1-specific TCR from peripheral blood of healthy donors. We stimulated these T cells with anti-CD3/CD28 Dynabeads for 1 day (transient stimulation) or 5 days (sustained stimulation), and observed upregulation of TIM-3, an inhibitory receptor with high expression in T cells from late-stage RCC tumors20,21, with sustained stimulation (Figure 4F, S9A, S9B). Stimulation of macrophages with IFNγ upregulated the expression of Gal-9 and PD-L1 (Figure 4G, S9C). We then cocultured RCC cell lines (A498, UOK127) expressing HLA-A*02:01 and the NY-ESO-1 antigen with T cells and IFNγ-stimulated or unstimulated macrophages (Methods). The cell lines were less efficiently killed by NY-ESO-1-T cells when IFNγ-stimulated macrophages were present in coculture, relative to when unstimulated macrophages were present (Figure 4H, S9D). Thus, prior exposure to IFNγ can enable a subset of myeloid cells to dampen RCC tumor cell killing by antigen-specific T cells.

## DISCUSSION:

Efforts to determine the net effect of IFNs on ICB outcomes in RCC have largely focused on the role of tumor-specific signaling on modulating response, with a general lack of agreement between model systems and patient clinical data17-19. In this study, we used scRNA-seq data from RCC patient cohorts to systematically describe IFN signaling within tumor, stromal, myeloid, and lymphoid cell types. Our approach for inferring the IFN-inducibility of genes in this context yielded cell type-specific signatures of type-I and type-II signaling, enabling more comprehensive modeling of outcomes under ICB-containing regimens.

We found that signatures of tumor and immune ISGs from melanoma showed different patterns of expression in RCC, suggesting a need for caution when applying gene programs derived from one disease context to another. In melanoma patient data, the expression of tumor ISGs (ISG.RS) predicts immunotherapy resistance14. However, this set of genes was lowly expressed in RCC malignant cells, indicating that tumor-expressed mechanisms of IFN-driven immune evasion described in other cancer types may be less impactful in the renal setting. Moreover, immune ISGs (IFNG.GS), which predict immunotherapy response in melanoma, were heterogeneous in RCC, with drastically different expression patterns between myeloid and T/NK cells.

In IFNγ-rich tumors, RCC TAMs were polarized towards a CXCL10-Hi state defined also by upregulation of genes encoding inhibitory immune checkpoints such as CD274, PDCD1LG2, LGALS9, NECTIN2, and TNFRSF14. Even at pre-treatment baseline, immune checkpoint genes were highly expressed and IFN-driven in TAMs, and less so in RCC tumor cells. Although further efforts are necessary to determine whether these transcriptional measurements correspond to protein expression, our results are aligned with prior reports of inhibitory ligand expression patterns in other disease types, e.g. MSI-H colon cancer, where the majority of PD-L1 expression is by myeloid cells, not tumor cells70. Indeed, immune cell PD-L1 positivity is more predictive of response to checkpoint blockade than tumor PD-L1 positivity in several cancers71-74, pointing to the functional significance of myeloid inhibitory ligand expression in modulating the anti-tumor response.

Type-II IFN is known to induce PD-L1 expression by both tumor and immune cells12. Here, we found that IFN signaling in RCC TAMs also drives the expression of ligands for TIM-3, TIGIT, and BTLA, as well as expression of anti-phagocytic checkpoints such as SIGLEC10 and LILRB1. We demonstrated in multiple orthogonal RCC patient cohorts that myeloid IFNγ signaling, not tumor IFNγ signaling, predicts shorter PFS and lack of clinical benefit under ICB plus anti-VEGF regimens. Finally, we showed that IFNy-stimulated macrophages dampen T cell killing of RCC tumor cells in vitro. Overall, these findings expand upon the known immunosuppressive effects of IFN signaling, and challenge the notion that IFNy polarizes macrophages in the TME towards a solely pro-inflammatory, anti-tumor, M1-like phenotype.

Indeed, IFNγ signaling in myeloid cells is crucial for several anti-tumor functions, including recruitment of T cells via chemokine production, T cell co-stimulation, and antigen presentation. However, the net negative impact of myeloid type-II signaling on RCC clinical outcomes may suggest that these IFN-driven effects are less critical in late stage RCC tumors, where CD8 T cell infiltration and activation are extensive at baseline. In this highly inflamed setting, IFNγ-exposed myeloid cells could instead act as a significant barrier to anti-tumor immunity, as CD8 T cells invigorated by checkpoint blockade are met with an abundance of inhibitory ligands, thereby constraining the proliferative burst necessary for ICB response.

Future work should also focus on the development of in vivo models appropriate for interrogating the immune phenotypes described herein. To date, RCC lacks an immunologically faithful mouse model, with existing syngeneic models such as Renca and LVRCC67 failing to fully recapitulate key genetic, histologic, and immune features of human RCC75-77. The continued development of in vivo systems will be crucial for understanding the functional dynamics of IFNγ-mediated cell states and their net impact on antitumor immunity in this disease.

Our study points towards type-II IFN signaling in myeloid cells as a tumor-extrinsic mediator of resistance to immunotherapy in RCC. Although ICB-containing regimens have become standard-of-care in first-line management of this disease, most patients do not exhibit durable responses1-6. Unlike in other cancers, signatures of immune inflammation do not consistently predict improved clinical outcomes8,10. Our findings suggest that high baseline levels of IFNγ in RCC tumors can condition myeloid cells, especially macrophages, to constrain T cell function under checkpoint blockade. Thus, we nominate a targetable pathway and cell type for combating primary resistance to ICB plus anti-VEGF therapy in advanced RCC patients.

## LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY:

Although this study integrates data for 42 RCC tumor samples across three independent cohorts, dataset size remains a notable limitation. Low cell numbers for less frequent cell types resulted in a lack of statistical power in discovery of CTS ISGs for stromal cell types and plasma cells. We note also that some ISGs involved in mechanisms of immune evasion may be strongly expressed across multiple cell types; our signature derivation approach, in prioritizing highly cell type-specific biology, does not identify such genes.

Moreover, our method for deriving CTS ISGs failed to identify a reproducible signature of tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β signaling, perhaps due to substantial tumor-to-tumor heterogeneity in the type-I IFN response. Among tumor cells in our integrated dataset, a small number of samples showed drastically high IFNα/β CytoSig scores, which could be driven by endogenous type-I IFN production78. However, IFNα and IFNβ gene transcripts are detected at near-zero levels in conventional scRNA-seq data, and the activation of cytosolic RNA/DNA sensing pathways is not directly measurable by transcriptional profiling. Therefore, our understanding of the sources and effects of type-I IFN in RCC malignant cells is incomplete, and our ability to model the relationship between tumoral IFNα/β signaling and ICB response using bulk RNA-seq data is limited. Our negative findings with respect to tumor and fibroblast type-I IFN signaling in predicting ICB outcomes may reflect limitations in our signatures, and do not preclude the possibility of a role for tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β signaling in modulating antitumor immunity. Further experimental efforts are needed to identify mechanisms upstream and downstream of type-I IFN signaling in RCC tumors, and to inform an understanding of their impact on ICB efficacy.

### METHODS

#### Preprocessing of scRNA-seq data

FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Bi and He et al. cohort were obtained from dbGap (accession number phs002065.v1.p1)20. FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Braun et al. cohort were obtained from dbGap (accession number phs002252.v1.p1)21. FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Krishna et al. cohort were obtained from the Sequence Read Archive (accession number PRJNA705464)22.

Barcode processing, read alignment, and UMI counting were performed using the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger analysis pipeline v6.0.1. Reads were aligned to the human genome reference b37 with the GENCODE 30 annotation lifted over to GRCh3779. Confidently mapped, non-PCR duplicate reads were counted to generate a gene-barcode matrix for each sample.

To abrogate sample-to-sample technical variability arising from cell-free RNA profiles, we performed ambient RNA decontamination on each sample from the three cohorts using CellBender v0.2.080. Raw counts for each sample were provided as input to the remove-background module of CellBender. Remove-background was run on all samples using the “full” model, 150 training epochs, and 25,000 total droplets included. For each sample, the expected cells parameter was derived from the estimated number of cells from Cell Ranger, rounded up to the nearest hundred. All other remove-background parameters were kept as default.

We performed multiplet detection and removal on CellBender-cleaned counts matrices using Scrublet v0.2.181. For each sample, the expected doublet rate parameter was set to 0.1. Doublet score thresholds were then selected manually to separate putative singlet and neotypic doublet modes in the distribution of simulated doublet scores. Predicted doublets were subsequently removed from each sample, yielding singlet-only, ambient RNA-cleaned counts matrices for downstream analysis in the Seurat R package v4.2.082.

Prior to further quality control and cell type annotation, all samples (42 total) were merged into a single Seurat object. Genes detected in fewer than three cells across samples were removed. Cells with fewer than 200 features detected or 25% or more of counts from mitochondrially-encoded transcripts were also removed. Raw counts were then normalized using the default Seurat log-normalization method. The top 2000 variable genes were identified using mean-variance standardized feature values (FindVariableFeatures function in Seurat with selection.method = “vst”). Data were scaled and principal components analysis (PCA) was performed on the scaled data. To unify samples across cohorts, we performed integration using the Harmony R package v0.1.083 on the top 50 principal components (PCs), adjusting for cohort of origin and sample as covariates. The 50 Harmony-corrected dimensions were then used for unsupervised Louvain clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP).

#### Identification of malignant cells

Malignant cells were identified using inferred copy number profiles and cluster-level expression of canonical RCC tumor marker genes. For each sample, cells passing quality control were subsetted from the integrated Seurat object and data were re-normalized and re-scaled following feature selection as described. PCA was performed on the scaled data and the top 30 PCs were used for Louvain clustering and UMAP. Louvain clusters were annotated as broad cell types based on a panel of canonical marker genes for immune, stromal, and tumor cells. We then performed InferCNV (https://github.com/broadinstitute/inferCNV) on each sample, using putative tumor and stromal clusters as observation groups and immune clusters as reference groups. Malignant clusters were identified in InferCNV outputs based on clear patterns of copy number gain or loss, as well as known CNV features of RCC such as chromosome 3p loss. For samples where one or more clusters showed substantial heterogeneity in inferred copy number profiles, we performed an additional iteration of subsetting, normalization, scaling, PCA, and clustering for cells in the clusters of interest to resolve further cell states. We then reran InferCNV for said samples incorporating these more granular states to arrive at malignant cell calls.

These InferCNV results were then cross-referenced with broad cell type calls performed on Louvain clusters in the full integrated dataset. One cluster in particular showed highly specific expression of RCC tumor marker genes such as CRYAB, CLU, NDUFA4L2, and CA9. Cells in this cluster constituted 97.47% of cells labeled via InferCNV as malignant. Thus, cancer cells were definitively called as the overlap between cells in this cluster and cells identified as malignant using copy number profiles from InferCNV. Additionally, we excluded from downstream analysis all cells in this cluster labeled by InferCNV as non-malignant, and all cells not in this cluster (immune and stromal) labeled by InferCNV as malignant.

#### Annotation of cell types and subtypes

Annotation of granular tumor, immune, and stromal cell subtypes was performed via iterations of subsetting, normalization, feature selection, scaling, PCA, Harmony integration, Louvain clustering, and differential expression analysis within broad cell types.

For example, to annotate lymphoid cell subtypes, we first subsetted the integrated data to Louvain clusters labeled broadly as T cell, NK-like T cell, NK, T-reg, B cell, and plasma cell based on canonical marker expression, as well as lymphoid cells from a mixed cluster comprised of cycling cells from different immune lineages. Clustering and differential expression analysis within this lymphoid subset allowed for the identification of more high resolution states, including multiple groups of CD8 T cells and T-helper cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), as well as groups of cells with low quality-control metrics and/or ambiguous marker gene expression. For this level of annotation, differential expression analysis was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “wilcox”) with Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Subsequent iterations of subsetting, for example to only CD8 T cells or only T-helper cells, further clarified granular cell states and enabled identification of low quality/ambiguous/contaminating cells. Lastly, to achieve cell subtype annotations without any influence of low quality/ambiguous/contaminating cells, we performed a final iteration of subsetting and clustering on each individual lymphoid cell type (CD8 T cell, T-helper, T-reg, NK, B and plasma cell), excluding poor quality cells. For this final level of annotation, differential expression analysis was performed using a logistic regression framework (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”) with Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing. The highly granular annotations obtained via these subsetted objects were then mapped back onto the full integrated dataset and used to re-define broad cell types among high quality cells only.

We applied this approach to lymphoid and myeloid lineages, as well as stromal and tumor cells, resulting in a final set of 228,371 high quality total cells across 14 broad cell types (tumor, fibroblast, perivascular, endothelial, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8 T cell, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, T-reg, B cell, and plasma cell) (Table S1A).

#### Single cell signature scoring

All single cell signature scoring was performed on normalized data using the combined z-score approach (“zscore” method parameter) implemented by the hacksig R package v0.1.284,85.

#### Defining putative ISGs

Putative ISGs were defined as the union of genes from the HALLMARK_INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE and HALLMARK_INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE gene sets from MSigDB, the IFNG.GS and ISG.RS gene sets from Benci et al14, and a curated set of genes encoding inhibitory ligands, immune checkpoints, and other immune evasion factors with prior evidence for being regulated by IFN signaling (Table S1D).

#### Inferring IFN-inducibility of genes

To infer the IFN-inducibility of genes in our dataset, we first used CytoSig v126 to quantify relative type-I and type-II IFN signaling at single cell resolution within each cell type. For a given broad cell type, we provided a normalized, mean-centered expression matrix containing cells of that type and all genes in the dataset as input to CytoSig. Because fibroblasts and perivascular cells showed highly similar expression profiles in our data, these two cell types were combined into a single group for CytoSig scoring and IFN-inducibility inference. We ran CytoSig with default parameters to obtain scores for IFNα/β and IFNγ cytokine signaling activity in cells of each cell type. For later analyses requiring binning of cells into discrete IFNα/β or IFNγ signaling low and high groups, we considered cells with a CytoSig z-score > 0 and CytoSig p-value < 0.05 as signaling-high and cells with a CytoSig z-score < 0 and CytoSig p-value < 0.05 as signaling-low.

Next, for a given gene, we fit a linear mixed effects model within cells of a given broad cell type for predicting normalized expression using IFNα/β CytoSig score, IFNγ CytoSig score, number of genes detected per cell, early (I/II) versus late (III/IV) disease stage, and patient of origin as predictor variables. In these models, patient of origin was considered a random effect, and all other variables were considered fixed effects. Models were fit using the lmer function from the lmerTest R package v3.1.386. β coefficients for IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores in these models represent IFN inducibility, i.e. the extent to which relative type I and type II IFN signaling levels predict the expression of a given gene. We fit these models for all putative ISGs and a set of highly variable genes. Here, highly variable genes were defined as the union of the top 2000 most variable genes across all cell types and the top 2000 variable genes within each broad cell type as determined using the FindVariableFeatures function in Seurat with selection.method = “vst”. Across these mixed effects models, p-values for IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores were adjusted using Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Genes with an IFNα/β CytoSig score β coefficient > 0 and BH-adjusted p < 0.01 were considered type-I-inducible, while genes with an IFNγ CytoSig score β coefficient > 0 and BH-adjusted p < 0.01 were considered type-II-inducible.

We applied this approach for inferring the IFN-inducibility of genes within cell types using (a) the full integrated dataset (Table S2A-S2M) and (b) cells from previously untreated patients only, describing IFN-driven variability in gene expression at baseline before first-line therapy (Table S3A-S3M).

#### Determining sources of IFNs in RCC tumors

To identify cell types and subtypes contributing IFNγ to the RCC microenvironment, we applied multiple linear regression models to predict IFNγ signaling levels across samples using CD8, CD8 NK-like, and NK cell proportions and IFNG expression as explanatory variables (Figure S3B).

For a given broad cell type, we calculated the median IFNγ CytoSig score and median IFNα/β CytoSig score within each sample. We then fit a multiple linear regression model for predicting median IFNγ CytoSig scores using the proportion of CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells in each sample, the percentages of CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells in each sample expressing IFNG with greater than 0 normalized counts, and median IFNα/β CytoSig scores as predictor variables. We fit these regression models for each broad cell type in the dataset. Again, because fibroblasts and perivascular cells showed highly similar expression profiles in our data, these two cell types were combined into a single group for this analysis. Models were fit using the lm function from the base stats R package v4.1.0.

To pinpoint the source of IFNγ to granular CD8 subsets, we applied a similar modeling approach. Again, for a given broad cell type, we calculated the median IFNγ CytoSig score and median IFNα/β CytoSig score within each sample. We then fit a multiple linear regression for predicting median IFNγ CytoSig scores using the proportion of CD8 41BB-Hi, CD8 LAG3-Hi, CD8 HSP-Hi, CD8 ISG-Hi, and CD8 IL7R-Hi cells in each sample, the percentages of CD8 41BB-Hi, CD8 LAG3-Hi, CD8 HSP-Hi, CD8 ISG-Hi, and CD8 IL7R-Hi cells in each sample expressing IFNG with greater than 0 normalized counts, and median IFNα/β CytoSig scores as predictor variables. Cycling CD8 subsets (CD8 Cyc. 1, CD8 Cyc. 2, CD8 Cyc.4), subsets comprised primarily of cells from a single sample (CD8 TRBV5-6-Hi, CD8 TRBV3-1-Hi), subsets consisting of less than 2000 cells (CD8 KLRB1-Hi, CD8 FOXP3-Hi, CD8 TRBV7-7-Hi), and a subset with low nFeatures and nCounts per cell and defined by genes encoding ribosomal subunits (CD8 RPS-Hi) were not considered in this analysis. We again fit these regression models for each broad cell type in the dataset.

We then attempted to determine cell types contributing IFNα/β to the RCC microenvironment using a similar approach. For each broad cell type, we fit a multiple linear regression for predicting median IFNα/β CytoSig scores using the proportion of TAMs, monocytes, DCs, tumor cells, endothelial cells, and perivascular cells and fibroblasts, as well as median IFNγ CytoSig scores as predictor variables. In these models, tumor cell proportion appeared to consistently predict IFNα/β CytoSig scores across cell types. However, closer inspection of the data revealed that these results could be driven by samples from a single patient from the Krishna et al cohort (patient UT2). Upon omitting these samples and re-fitting our linear models, we found that no broad cell type proportion was consistently significantly predictive of type-I IFN signaling (Figure S3D-S3F).

#### Derivation of IFN signaling signatures

We defined gene signatures of cell type-specific type-I and type-II IFN signaling based on criteria for both cell type specificity and IFN inducibility using cells from ICB-naive patients only.

First, we established groups of broad cell types based on similar patterns of putative ISG expression. TAMs, monocytes, and DCs formed one group (myeloid), CD8, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, and T-reg formed another (T/NK), and tumor cells and perivascular cells/fibroblasts formed a third group (tumor/fibroblast).

For a given broad cell type, we identified cell type-specific (CTS) genes by performing a series of pairwise one-versus-each differential expression tests between that cell type and all other cell types. Differential expression testing was performed using the FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”. Early (I/II) versus late (III/IV) disease stage and patient of origin were incorporated as latent variables; p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. A gene was considered cell type-specific only if it passed the following cutoffs in all pairwise tests (excluding tests between cell types in the same group): average log2FC > 0, pctCOI - pctComp > 0, pctComp < 20, and Bonferroni adjusted p-value < 0.05. Here, pctCOI represents the percentage of cells in the cell type of interest expressing the gene at greater than 0 normalized counts, and pctComp represents the percentage of cells in the comparator cell type expressing the gene at greater than 0 normalized counts.

For each broad cell type, we then identified the overlap of CTS genes with significantly type-I or type-II-inducible putative ISGs in that cell type as determined by our mixed effects modeling approach in cells from ICB-naive patients. These CTS, significantly IFN-inducible genes were then combined across cell types of the same group to arrive at signatures of myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β and IFNγ signaling (Figure S5C, Table S1D), which were then used for clinical outcomes analysis in IM151 and JR101.

TAM, monocyte, and DC non-IFN-inducible signatures were initially defined as CTS genes for which the abs(β coefficient) of both IFNα/β CytoSig score and IFNγ CytoSig score were < 0.1 and corresponding BH-adjusted p-value > 0.1. These signatures were then filtered to exclude genes with IFNα/β CytoSig score or IFNγ CytoSig score β coefficient > 0.1 and corresponding BH-adjusted p-value < 0.05 in any of the three myeloid cell types (TAM, monocyte, or DC).

#### Derivation of expanded IFN signaling signatures

The myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β and IFNγ signaling signatures described above were constrained to our pre-defined set of 259 putative ISGs, primarily grounded in the highly canonical Hallmark IFNγ response and Hallmark IFNα response gene-sets. However, a more comprehensive set of putative ISGs can be derived from experimental datasets. We therefore expanded our set of putative ISGs using genes exhibiting consistent IFNγ or IFNα/β inducibility in the CytoSig treatment response database, then used this expanded set to re-identify cell type-specific ISG signatures using our same criteria for cell type specificity and interferon inducibility (Figure S10A-S10F). We then examined the association between these expanded signatures and ICB outcomes in IM151 and JR101 (Figure S10G-S10J).

First, we obtained the data matrix of cytokine treatment responses (weighted log2FC) and meta information for each treatment profile from the CytoSig web portal (https://cytosig.ccr.cancer.gov/)26. We then subsetted the treatment response data to either IFNγ-treated experiments or IFNα/β-treated experiments. For each experiment, we manually annotated the broad cell type of the tested cell model, and only considered experiments in broad cell types with relevance to our study (cell types such as neuroblastoma, and placenta were excluded, for example).

For IFNγ-treated experiments, we considered the following broad cell types: B cell, DC, macrophage, monocyte, endothelial, fibroblast, proximal tubule epithelial, melanoma, and lung adenocarcinoma. For IFNα/β-treated experiments, we considered the following cell types: B cell, DC, endothelial, fibroblast, macrophage, monocyte, T cell, melanoma, and lung adenocarcinoma. The inclusion of melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma cell lines for this analysis was intended to help retrieve additional tumor/epithelial-expressed ISGs. For each broad cell type, we then identified all genes with a weighted log2FC > 1.5 in greater than 50% of experiments within that broad cell type. Exceptions were made for broad cell types with just 2 or 3 experiments; for these, genes were retained if they had a weighted log2FC > 1.5 in greater than 1 experiment. We performed this analysis separately for IFNg-treated and IFNa/b-treated experiments. Under this approach, we identified 118 putative ISGs not present in our original 259-gene putative ISG set.

Using this expanded putative ISG set (377 genes total) (Table S1D), we re-derived myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFN signaling signatures using the approach described above. The inclusion of these additional putative ISGs from CytoSig resulted in only a single new signature gene for tumor/fibroblasts (DSP, an IFNγ-inducible gene) and no new signature genes for T and NK cells (Figure S10A, S10B, Table S1D). However, several new IFNγ and IFNα/β signaling signature genes were identified for myeloid cells (Figure S10A, S10B, Table S1D). In myeloid cells, SLAMF8, PSTPIP2, and FCGR1B emerged as IFNg-only ISGs. IL1RN, C1QB, and SIGLEC1 emerged as IFNα/β-only ISGs. TNFSF13B, FPR2, and ANKRD22 emerged as both IFNγ-inducible and IFNα/β-inducible myeloid ISGs. These expanded signatures exhibited patterns of expression similar to our original signatures in single cell samples not used for signature discovery and in bulk RNA-seq data (Figure S10C-S10F).

We then asked whether these expanded signatures were predictive of immunotherapy outcomes in IM151 and JR101. Consistent with our original signatures, the myeloid IFNγ signaling expanded signature, but not the tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling expanded signature, was associated with poorer outcomes under ICB plus anti-VEGF in IM151 and JR101 (Figure S10G-S10J). Thus, models employing the expanded signatures still primarily implicate myeloid IFNγ signaling as a predictor of immunotherapy resistance, and do not drastically deviate from the results obtained using our original signatures. We provide both the original and expanded signatures for readers in Table S1D.

#### Bulk RNA-seq signature scoring and deconvolution

Raw sequencing data and associated clinical metadata for the JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort were obtained from published results63,64. Paired-end bulk RNA-seq samples were realigned to the hg19 genome reference using STAR v2.7.087, with alignment parameters --outFilterMultimapNmax 20 --outFilterMismatchNmax 999 --outFilterMismatchNoverReadLmax 0.04 --alignIntronMin 20 --alignIntronMax 1250000 --alignMatesGapMax 1250000. Sequencing primers were removed with cutadapt88, gene expression was quantified using RSEM89 v1.3.1, and duplicate reads were marked using Picard’s Mark Duplicates (https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/). Quality control metrics were extracted using RNA-SeQC290. For each sample, we obtained the number of genes detected (GD), the estimated library size, the end 1 sense rate (E1SR), the end 2 sense rate (E2SR) and exonic rate from RNA-SeQC2. For each sample, we also calculated the gene interquartile range (IQR) as previously described91 to estimate the dynamic range of gene expression. First, potential sample outliers in gene expression space were detected by PCA analysis of TPM-normalized expression values. We plotted the above quality metrics stratified by potential outliers versus potentially quality control passing samples, and were able to determine the most appropriate thresholds. The following thresholds provided the best outlier detection: GD ≤ 16000, geneIQRs ≤ 0, E2SR ≥ 0.1, E1SR ≤ 0.85.

Recurrent copy number variants (CNVs) in whole-exome sequencing samples from JAVELIN Renal 101 were determined using GISTIC2.092, v2.0.23, with the following input parameters: amplification threshold=0.1, deletion threshold=0.1, q-value threshold=0.1, cap values=1.5, broad length cutoff=0.7, confidence level=0.99, join segment size=20, arm level peel off=1, maximum sample segments=800, gene collapse method=mean, including matched normals as reference.

Processed bulk RNA-seq data and associated clinical metadata from the IMmotion151 cohort were obtained from published results (European Genome-Phenome Archive: EGAS00001004353)61,62.

All signature scoring in bulk RNA-seq data was performed on normalized TPM matrices using the combined z-score approach (“zscore” method parameter) implemented by the hacksig R package v0.1.284,85. Apart from signatures derived in this study, signatures describing various immune cell states and phenotypes were obtained from previously published studies17,22,64,67,69.

To infer cell type proportions in bulk RNA-seq samples, we performed deconvolution using CIBERSORTx Fractions via the CIBERSORTx docker and source code65. First, we constructed a reference using ICB-naive samples in our single cell data. We downsampled this subset of the data to a maximum of 3000 cells from each broad cell type. We then removed all genes encoding mitochondrial transcripts and ribosomal proteins (RPS and RPL genes), as well as genes with 0 total counts across the downsampled data. We ran CIBERSORTx Fractions using non-logged TPM matrices for the IMmotion151 and JAVELIN Renal 101 bulk RNA-seq data as mixture files, the downsampled, gene-filtered, non-logged single cell reference expression matrix as the refsample, S-mode batch correction, no quantile normalization, and 1 permutation (CIBERSORTx p-values were not used for downstream analysis).

#### Clinical outcomes analysis

Cox proportional hazards (PH) analysis and Kaplan-Meier analysis were performed using the survival v3.2.11 and survminer v0.4.9.999 R packages. To determine the relationship between baseline levels of cell type-specific IFN signaling and outcomes under first-line ICB plus anti-VEGF therapy, we fit multivariate Cox proportional hazards models for progression-free survival (PFS) in each treatment arm of IMmotion151 and JAVELIN Renal 101 using the coxph function. These models incorporated as predictor variables myeloid IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

Further inspection of models fitted in the ICB plus anti-VEGF arms of both studies revealed mild violations of the proportional hazards assumption for some variables (determined using the cox.zph function of the survival R package). Schoenfeld residuals were visualized using the coxzphplot function of the autoReg R package v0.3.4. In a Cox model for PFS in the atezolizumab plus bevacizumab treatment arm of IMmotion151, MSKCC risk group, TAM fraction, and DC fraction showed statistically significant violation of the PH assumption (Table S4C). However, stratification of the model by MSKCC risk group using the strata function in the survival R package did not substantially affect the hazard ratio or associated p-value of key predictor variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.59, 95% C.I. = 1.21–2.09, p < 0.001; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.51, 95% C.I. = 0.35-0.72, p < 0.001) (Table S4D, S4E). Removal of all cell type fractions from the stratified model (resolving all violations of the PH assumption) also had no substantial effect on the HR or p-value of these variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.66, 95% C.I. = 1.30-2.12, p < 0.001; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.58, 95% C.I. = 0.45-0.75, p < 0.001) (Table S4F, S4G).

In a Cox model for PFS in the avelumab plus axitinib treatment arm of JAVELIN Renal 101, only patient age showed statistically significant violation of the PH assumption (Table S4H). Removal of age from the model (resolving all violations of the PH assumption) had no substantial effect on the HR or p-value of key variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.50, 95% C.I. = 1.03-2.17, p = 0.033; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.56, 95% C.I. = 0.37-0.85, p = 0.007) (Table S4I, S4J).

For Kaplan-Meier analysis, optimal cutoffs for Krishna CD8 predictive and myeloid IFNγ signaling signatures were established using the surv_cutpoint function from the survminer R package with the minprop parameter set to 0. In the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arm of each study, we first applied surv_cutpoint on the Krishna CD8 predictive signature and defined samples as signature-low or signature-high based on the optimal threshold. Within Krishna CD8 predictive-high samples in the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arm, we then applied surv_cutpoint on the myeloid IFNγ signaling signature and defined samples as signature-low or signature-high based on the optimal threshold. These same thresholds were applied to the sunitinib treatment arm of each study. We then assessed the effect of myeloid IFNγ signaling on PFS as a categorical variable (high/low) in multivariate and univariate Cox models in each arm of the two studies. For multivariate analysis, predictor variables included myeloid IFNγ signaling as a categorical variable, TAM, monocyte, and DC fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

Multivariate logistic regression analysis for predicting clinical benefit (CB) versus no clinical benefit (NCB) was performed using the glm function from the base stats R package v4.1.0 with the family parameter set to “binomial”. Patients with clinical benefit were defined as those with an objective response of CR, PR, or SD with PFS greater than or equal to 6 months. Patients with no clinical benefit were defined as those with an objective response of PD or SD with PFS less than 6 months. These logistic regression models incorporated as predictor variables myeloid IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

To assess the effect of non-ISG or external myeloid signatures on clinical outcomes, we fit a series of multivariate Cox models for PFS and logistic regression models for CB versus NCB in the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arms of both studies. These models incorporated as predictor variables a given myeloid signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models. The variance inflation factor (VIF) for each variable in these models was calculated using the car R package v3.1.1. Only models where the VIF of all variables was less than 10 were considered valid for this analysis.

#### NY-ESO-1 TCR transduction

We generated retrovirus encoding an NY-ESO-1–specific TCR (pMX vector harboring IRES-GFP) using a standard two-step packaging strategy and introduced it into human T cells, adapted from a published protocol93. First, Phoenix-GPE packaging cells were transfected with the vector using TransIT-LT1 (Mirus Bio, #MIR 2304). After 24 hours, the supernatant was collected. The filtered supernatant was then used to transduce PG13 cells in the presence of polybrene (MilliporeSigma, #TR-1003-G), with spin infection to enhance viral entry. Following a brief incubation, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium, and PG13 cells were expanded to obtain virus-containing supernatant. Human T cells were isolated from cryopreserved healthy-donor PBMCs by negative selection using a biotinylated antibody cocktail and magnetic beads (Miltenyi Biotec, Pan T cell isolation kit, #130-096-535). Purified cells were resuspended in T-cell medium and activated with 20 IU/ml IL-2 (Miltenyi Biotec, #130-097-745). Activation was performed by seeding T cells into wells pre-coated with anti-CD3 antibody (Biolegend, #317325) and RetroNectin (Takara Bio USA, #T100B). For TCR transfer, PG13-derived viral supernatant was loaded onto plates pretreated with RetroNectin and anti-CD3 and centrifuged to adsorb virions to the substrate, after which pre-activated T cells were seeded onto the virus-bound plates. Spin introduction was applied and then cells were subsequently cultured at 37 °C in 5% CO2 in IL-2–supplemented medium. Transduction efficiency was assessed approximately one week later by flow-cytometric quantification of GFP positivity among live cells. For experiments using chronically stimulated T cells, cells were generated by once-daily stimulation for five consecutive days prior to use.

#### Stimulation of monocyte-derived macrophages

Human monocytes were isolated from healthy-donor PBMCs by positive selection using CD14 MicroBeads according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Miltenyi Biotec, CD14 MicroBeads, #130-050-201). Purified CD14 cells were cultured at 37 °C in 5% CO2 in RPMI medium supplemented with recombinant human M-CSF (50 ng/mL) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #PHC9504) to induce differentiation into monocyte-derived macrophages. Differentiation was continued until cells displayed adherent macrophage morphology within 7 days. The macrophage phenotype was verified by flow cytometry as CD11b+CD33+CD163+. For activation, differentiated macrophages were either left unstimulated (control) or primed with recombinant human IFN-γ (10 ng/mL) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #PHC4031) for 24 h. Both unstimulated and IFN-γ-stimulated macrophages were subsequently used in the killing assays described below.

#### In vitro cytotoxicity assay

We tested cytotoxic activity using a luciferase assay as described previously94. To assess T-cell cytotoxicity, we established an antigen-specific killing assay using NY-ESO-1 (CTAG1B) as the model antigen. The human RCC cell lines UOK-127 and A498 (both HLA-A*02:01–positive) were used as target cells. The luciferase gene and CTAG1B gene (encoding NY-ESO-1) were introduced into cell lines using a lentivirus system, and T cells were engineered to express the NY-ESO-1–specific T cell receptor restricted by HLA-A*02:01 (NY-ESO-1 T cells) using a retroviral system as described above. In the killing assay, the genetically-engineered RCC cell lines (5.0 × 104 cells per well) were co-cultured with NY-ESO-1 T cells at 1:1 or 3:1 effector to target ratios and IFNγ-stimulated macrophages or unstimulated macrophages (1.5 × 105 cells), or no macrophages for 18 hours. To measure the cytotoxic activity of NY-ESO-1 T cells, a luciferase substrate (Promega, Bright-Glo™ Luciferase Assay System, #E2610) was directly added to each well. Emitted light was detected in a SpectraMax M3 (Molecular Devices). Lysis was determined as (1 – (RLUsample)/(RLUmax)) × 100.

Single cell suspensions from induced macrophages were blocked with Human TruStain FcX™ (Biolegend, #422302). Single cell suspensions from T cells were stained with the following anti-human antibodies and the brilliant stain buffer (BD Biosciences): BUV737-CD45 (HI30, #568524), BUV395-CD3 (UCHT1, #563546), BV786-TIM-3 (344823, #747958), and BV421-TIGIT (741182, #747844) were purchased from BD Bioscience. ### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

Statistical analyses were performed using R v4.1.0 and GraphPad Prism. Statistical details (including sample size n) are reported in results, figures, figure legends, STAR methods, supplementary tables, and data analysis code in the public repository for this study (see Data and Code Availability). Inclusion/exclusion criteria for cells, signatures, samples, and clinical groupings for all analyses are described in detail in results and relevant STAR Methods sections. For all figures, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001.

Differential expression testing for initial cell type annotations was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method “wilcox”. Other differential expression analysis (final cell subset annotation, one-versus-each testing to identify CTS genes) was performed using a logistic regression framework and likelihood ratio test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”); early/late disease stage and patient were incorporated as latent variables and p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Significance testing for differences in signature scores between groups of cells or sample-level median scores between cell types was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. For all box plots, the centerline is the median, the box limits are upper and lower quartiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Linear mixed effects models for inferring the IFN-inducibility of individual genes were fit using the lmer function of the lmerTest R package v3.1.3; p-values for the IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig score variables were adjusted across models using Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Multiple linear regression models for inferring median IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores as a function of cell type proportions were fitted using the lm function of the base stats R package v4.1.0. Significance testing for differences in TAM subtype frequencies between groups of samples was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Error bars represent mean ± SD.

Significance testing for differences in signature scores between groups of bulk RNA-seq samples was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional-hazards models for progression-free survival were fit using the coxph function of the survival R package v3.2.11. Testing for violation of the proportional-hazards assumption in these models was performed using the cox.zph function of the survival R package and visualization of Schoenfeld residuals was performed using the coxzphplot function of the autoReg R package v0.3.4. Logistic regression models for predicting clinical benefit versus no clinical benefit were fit using the glm function of the base stats R package v4.1.0. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed using the survfit and ggsurvplot functions, and optimal signature score cutoffs for stratification were determined using the surv_cutpoint function from the survminer R package v0.4.9.999.

Significance testing for differences in inhibitory ligand expression (mean fluorescence intensity) between IFNγ-stimulated and unstimulated macrophages was performed using a two-sided t-test. Error bars represent mean ± SEM. Significance testing for differences in lysis of RCC cells by T cells in co-culture with IFNγ-stimulated macrophages versus unstimulated macrophages was performed using a two-sided t-test. Values were normalized to lysis without macrophages. Error bars represent mean ± SEM.
